reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal dominant condition characterised by branchial (neck) skin defects, ocular anomalies, and distinctive facial features
The branchial defects are often erythematous, atrophic, or haemangioma-like skin lesions in the lower neck or behind the ears
Ocular findings include microphthalmia, coloboma, and lacrimal duct obstruction
A characteristic facial sign is an upper lip anomaly resembling a poorly healed cleft, sometimes termed a lip pseudocleft
Premature greying of the hair and pigmentary changes are recognised associations
It is caused by variants in TFAP2A, a transcription factor important in neural crest and ectodermal development
Renal anomalies and hearing loss may occur, so audiological and renal assessment are advisable
reference.pathophysiology: Branchio-oculo-facial syndrome is caused by heterozygous variants in TFAP2A, which encodes a transcription factor (activating enhancer-binding protein 2 alpha) that regulates development of neural crest cells and surface ectoderm. Because cranial neural crest and ectodermal derivatives form the branchial arches, facial structures, eyes, and pigment cells, impaired TFAP2A function disrupts these tissues and produces the characteristic branchial skin defects, ocular malformations, facial anomalies, and pigmentary changes. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable expressivity, and many cases arise de novo, so a negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis.
additionalDifferentials: Cleft lip from other syndromic or isolated causes
additionalInvestigations: Ophthalmological examination for microphthalmia, coloboma, and lacrimal obstruction
Renal ultrasound to detect urinary tract anomalies
Examination and imaging of branchial skin defects and any sinuses
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant recurrence risk
redFlags: Infected or discharging branchial sinus or cyst
Undetected hearing loss affecting language development
Feeding or airway difficulty related to facial and oral anomalies
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is generally normal and cognition is usually preserved; morbidity relates to the severity of ocular, renal, and hearing involvement and to the reconstructive needs of the facial and branchial defects.
pitfalls: Mistaking the branchial skin lesions for infantile haemangiomas or infected cysts
Interpreting the lip pseudocleft as a simple repaired cleft and missing the syndrome
Overlooking lacrimal duct obstruction as a cause of recurrent eye discharge
Failing to screen for renal anomalies and hearing loss
Not offering genetic counselling given dominant inheritance
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Surgical reconstruction of the branchial neck skin defects and the upper lip pseudocleft
Ophthalmological management of microphthalmia and coloboma, and probing or surgery for lacrimal duct obstruction
Audiological rehabilitation with hearing aids for hearing loss
Renal assessment and management of any associated urinary tract anomalies
Multidisciplinary developmental follow-up across clinical genetics, ophthalmology, ENT and plastic surgery
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity, noting that many cases arise de novo
